title: Making Models Unmergeable via Scaling-Sensitive Loss Landscape
claim: Post-hoc, architecture-specific protections leave released weights mergeable; our training-time protection works across architectures and makes unauthorized merging fail.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: provider upload flow, protection methods, protected vs unprotected merge outcomes
description: A three-column figure. The left panel, labeled Provider, shows a developer with a laptop who trains a neural network and uploads it to a cloud showing GitHub and Hugging Face logos. Dashed arrows lead into the middle panel. The middle panel's top section, 'Training-time Protection (ours)', has a green lock and two sub-boxes: Architecture-Agnostic (a purple graph) and Low-Rank Adaptation (frozen W, trainable B and A matrices). Its bottom dotted section, 'Post-hoc Protection', has a red open lock and two boxes: Transformer (Q, K, V attention) and Full Fine-Tuning (W). The right panel has two rows. The top row, Protected Model + User Model with a green lock, reads 'Merging Fails → Unusable (TRAP!!!)'. The bottom row, Unprotected Model + User Model with a red open lock, reads 'Merging Succeeds → Usable (Unauthorized)'. Green and red separate good outcomes from bad ones.

abstract: The rise of model hubs has made it easier to access reusable model components, making model merging a practical tool for combining capabilities. Yet, this modularity also creates a governance gap: downstream users can recompose released weights into unauthorized mixtures that bypass safety alignment or licensing terms. Because existing defenses are largely post-hoc and architecture-specific, they provide inconsistent protection across diverse architectures and release formats in practice. To close this gap, we propose Trap$^2$, an architecture-agnostic protection framework that encodes protection into updates during fine-tuning, regardless of whether they are released as adapters or full models. Instead of relying on architecture-dependent approaches, Trap$^2$ uses weight re-scaling as a simple proxy for the merging process. It keeps released weights effective in standalone use, but degrades them under re-scaling that often arises in merging, undermining unauthorized recomposition.
